## Diagnostics, model adequacy, and follow-up comparisons

\includefigure{../output/figures/fig_part2_diagnostics.pdf}{Residual, normal Q--Q, scale-location, and Cook's-distance diagnostics for the two-factor model.}{fig:part2-diagnostics}

The Shapiro--Wilk test [@ShapiroWilk1965] detects a modest non-Gaussian departure
(\(W=`r p2_fmt(p2_shapiro$Statistic, 3)`\),
\(p=`r p2_fmt(p2_shapiro$P_value, 3)`\)); at \(n=1000\), this test is sensitive
to the discreteness and bounds of exam scores. The Brown--Forsythe test [@BrownForsythe1974] does not
reject equal within-cell variances
(\(F=`r p2_fmt(p2_bf$Statistic, 2)`\),
\(p=`r p2_fmt(p2_bf$P_value, 3)`\)). The conventional \(4/n\) influence rule
flags `r p2_influence_count` observations, but the maximum Cook's distance is
only `r p2_fmt(p2_max_cook, 4)`. HC3 robust standard errors preserve the same
decisions for both marginal effects and the interaction [@MacKinnonWhite1985].
Independence remains unverifiable because school and classroom identifiers are
absent; this is the main model-adequacy limitation.

Each factor has only two levels, so a within-factor Tukey procedure would merely
repeat its single main comparison. We instead report four scientifically direct
simple contrasts and control their familywise error with Holm's method
[@Holm1979].

\tightinputtable{../output/tables/tab_part2_simple_effects_display.tex}

All four simple contrasts remain significant after adjustment, but they are
secondary descriptions; the non-significant interaction remains the formal
test of whether the preparation association differs by lunch group.
